WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The United States needs a new law requiring that the president consult with Congress before going to war, a blue-ribbon panel led by two former secretaries of state said Tuesday. James Baker, left, and Warren Christopher led a panel that recommended a new War Powers Act. The current War Powers Resolution is "ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced," James Baker said in a joint appearance with Warren Christopher, announcing the results of the study they led. The recommendation follows failed efforts by Democrats in Congress to put a stop to the war in Iraq or to put conditions on President Bush's conduct of it. Congress passed a joint resolution to authorize armed force against Iraq in 2002, but some Bush opponents say it should not have been interpreted as a blank check for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation. Baker, who served in George H.W. Bush's administration, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said their project was not prompted by any specific war, with Christopher adding that the commission had "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here." "We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict," Baker added. The existing law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since it was passed as a response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher said. It requires presidents to report regularly to Congress about ongoing conflicts, but the provision has been flouted. "No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973," former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, said Tuesday. The panel, formally called the National War Powers Commission, said a new law should be created requiring the president to consult with key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than a week, or within three days of doing so in the case of operations that need to be kept secret. It should also make clear exactly who the president needed to consult. The panel suggests that the president talk to "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." The new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher said. Congress, in turn, would have to declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days, they said. If a resolution of approval failed, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," but it was not clear that such an act would stop a war in progress. Christopher was unable to say in the news conference what practical effect congressional disapproval would have. Baker said the commission had been in touch with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as leaders of Congress. He declined to reveal what they thought of the proposal, but said: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction." Congress has not officially declared war since 1942, when the United States entered formal hostilities with the Axis powers in World War II. But since then, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq. The Constitution makes the president the commander in chief of the armed forces, but gives Congress the power to declare war and approve military budgets. Baker and Christopher's group included both Republicans and Democrats and held seven meetings over 14 months.

Baker, who served in the administration of George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that their project was not prompted by any specific war. Christopher noted that the commission had "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here."

"We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict," Baker added.

The existing law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since its enactment as a response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher observed. Though it requires presidents to report regularly to Congress about ongoing conflicts, this provision has consistently been disregarded.

"No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973," former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, remarked on Tuesday.

The panel, formally designated the National War Powers Commission, recommended the creation of a new law requiring the president to consult with key members of Congress before deploying troops into combat expected to last more than a week—or within three days of such deployment in the case of operations requiring secrecy. The law should also clearly specify precisely whom the president is obligated to consult.

The panel proposes that the president confer with "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." This new committee would maintain a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher explained. Congress, in turn, would be required to declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days.

Should a resolution of approval fail, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," though it remains unclear whether such a measure would halt a war already underway. Baker indicated that the commission had been in contact with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as with congressional leaders. While he declined to disclose their views on the proposal, he offered: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction."

Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, when the United States entered into formal hostilities with the Axis powers during World War II. In the decades since, however, presidents have dispatched troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada, and Iraq. The Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the armed forces, while vesting in Congress the power to declare war and approve military budgets.

James Baker and Warren Christopher, who spearheaded the study, appeared together to reveal their findings. Baker characterized the existing War Powers Resolution as "ineffective," stating that it "should be repealed and it should be replaced."

This recommendation comes on the heels of unsuccessful attempts by congressional Democrats to either halt the Iraq war or impose restrictions on how President Bush was managing it. Back in 2002, Congress approved a joint resolution sanctioning military force against Iraq. However, certain critics of Bush argue that this measure was never meant to serve as unlimited authorization for the U.S. to invade and occupy the nation on the Persian Gulf.

Baker, who worked in the administration of George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served during Bill Clinton's presidency, emphasized that no particular conflict inspired their work. Christopher noted that the commission had "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here." Baker echoed this sentiment, saying, "We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict."

According to both men, every president since the War Powers Resolution of 1973 became law -- a measure enacted in reaction to the Vietnam War -- has viewed it as unconstitutional. Though the resolution obligates presidents to provide Congress with regular updates on ongoing hostilities, this requirement has gone ignored. Republican committee member and former Sen. Slade Gorton pointed out on Tuesday that "No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973."

Officially known as the National War Powers Commission, the panel called for new legislation obligating the president to confer with essential congressional figures before deploying troops into combat anticipated to exceed one week. For operations requiring secrecy, this consultation would need to occur within three days of deployment. The proposed law would also specify precisely which individuals the president must consult.

Under the commission's proposal, the president would communicate with "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." Baker and Christopher explained that this new committee would maintain a permanent professional staff granted access to intelligence data.

For its part, Congress would be required to either declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within a 30-day window. Should that resolution of approval fail, any lawmaker could put forward a "resolution of disapproval" -- though whether such action could actually terminate an ongoing conflict remained uncertain. During the news conference, Christopher couldn't specify what real-world consequences congressional disapproval would carry.

Baker mentioned that the commission had reached out to the presidential campaigns of Democratic candidate Barack Obama and Republican candidate John McCain, along with congressional leadership. While he wouldn't disclose their opinions on the proposal, he did remark: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction."

The last time Congress formally declared war was in 1942, when America officially entered combat against the Axis powers during World War II. In the years since, however, presidents have deployed forces to nations such as Korea, Vietnam, Grenada, and Iraq. While the Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the military, it reserves for Congress the authority to declare war and to authorize defense spending.

The bipartisan group assembled by Baker and Christopher featured members from both parties and convened seven times across a span of 14 months.

# Bipartisan Panel Recommends New War Powers Legislation

A blue-ribbon panel led by former Secretaries of State James Baker and Warren Christopher has recommended the enactment of a new law requiring the president to consult with Congress before committing the nation to war. The recommendation represents a significant bipartisan effort to reshape the balance of war-making authority between the executive and legislative branches.

At the heart of the panel's findings is the conclusion that the existing War Powers Resolution of 1973 has proven ineffective and should be repealed and replaced with more workable legislation. According to the panel, the current law has failed to achieve its intended purpose of ensuring meaningful consultation between the president and Congress on matters of war.

The evidence supporting this conclusion is striking. Every president since the resolution's passage has regarded the measure as unconstitutional, and no president has ever made a formal submission to Congress under the resolution since it was adopted in 1973. This consistent pattern of noncompliance across administrations of both political parties underscores the fundamental weaknesses of the current framework.

Baker and Christopher were careful to emphasize that their study was not prompted by any specific conflict, nor did it target any particular war. Rather, the panel's work was intended to address a long-standing structural problem in the way the United States makes decisions about the use of military force.

Under the proposed law, the president would be required to consult with key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than a week, or, alternatively, within three days of committing forces to such action. This provision is designed to guarantee genuine dialogue between the branches of government while still preserving the president's ability to respond swiftly to urgent threats.

# A New Framework for War Powers: The Baker-Christopher Recommendation

A distinguished bipartisan panel, co-chaired by former secretaries of state James Baker and Warren Christopher, has issued a significant recommendation calling for the repeal of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 and its replacement with new legislation designed to strengthen the relationship between the executive and legislative branches when the nation goes to war.

## The Failure of the 1973 Law

The War Powers Resolution, passed in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, was intended to reassert congressional authority over the deployment of American military forces. However, in the decades since its enactment, the law has proven both ineffective and largely disregarded. Notably, every president since 1973—regardless of party—has declined to formally comply with its provisions, often questioning its constitutionality and refusing to acknowledge that its requirements applied to their military decisions. This persistent non-compliance has rendered the resolution a symbolic gesture rather than a meaningful check on presidential war-making power.

## The Proposed Alternative

To address these shortcomings, the blue-ribbon panel has proposed a new law that would establish clearer and more workable procedures for cooperation between the president and Congress. Under the proposed framework, the president would be required to consult with key congressional leaders before ordering troops into any significant combat operation expected to last more than one week. In circumstances where prior consultation is not feasible, the president would be obligated to engage in such consultation within three days of committing forces to combat.

## Addressing Constitutional Concerns

This recommendation seeks to resolve longstanding constitutional tensions surrounding the division of war powers between the branches of government. The Constitution grants Congress the authority to declare war while designating the president as commander in chief, creating an inherent ambiguity that has fueled debate for generations. By emphasizing genuine consultation rather than rigid procedural mandates that presidents have historically resisted, the panel's proposal aims to create a more realistic and enforceable mechanism—one that respects both the president's need for operational flexibility and Congress's constitutional role in decisions of war and peace.

The panel's work represents an effort to move beyond the failures of the past and establish a durable framework that both branches can accept and follow, thereby restoring accountability and shared responsibility to one of the gravest decisions a nation can make.

# Understanding the Dateline: WASHINGTON (CNN)

If you've ever read online news, you've likely encountered the familiar opening: **WASHINGTON (CNN)** — followed by "The..." and the rest of a breaking story. This standardized format is a hallmark of professional journalism, and it carries more meaning than casual readers might realize.

## The Dateline Explained

The word "WASHINGTON" at the start of an article is known as a **dateline**. It tells readers where the story originated or where the reporting took place. Washington, D.C., as the seat of the United States federal government, is one of the most common datelines in American news, appearing in coverage of Congress, the White House, the Supreme Court, and countless federal agencies.

## The CNN Byline

The parenthetical **(CNN)** identifies the news organization responsible for the reporting. The Cable News Network, founded in 1980 by Ted Turner, was the first television channel to provide 24-hour news coverage. Today, CNN operates across television, digital platforms, and social media, making its Washington bureau a central hub for political journalism.

## The Opening Sentence

The word "**The**" typically begins the article's lead sentence—the crucial first line designed to capture the essence of the story. Journalists are trained to pack the most important information into this opening, answering the classic questions of who, what, when, where, and why.

## Why This Format Matters

This structure serves several purposes:

- **Credibility:** Readers immediately know the source and location of the news.
- **Consistency:** A standardized format helps audiences quickly parse information.
- **Transparency:** Attribution builds trust and accountability in reporting.

In an era of information overload and misinformation, understanding these small but meaningful conventions helps readers become more informed and critical consumers of the news.

# Bipartisan Commission Urges Overhaul of War Powers Law

**Former Secretaries of State Baker and Christopher Lead Call for New Framework on Military Action**

WASHINGTON (CNN) — A bipartisan commission co-chaired by former Secretaries of State James Baker and Warren Christopher has recommended replacing the 1973 War Powers Resolution with new legislation designed to clarify the roles of the president and Congress in decisions to send American troops into combat.

The commission, which spent more than a year studying the contentious issue, concluded that the decades-old law has failed to achieve its central purpose of ensuring collective judgment between the executive and legislative branches before the nation goes to war.

"The War Powers Resolution has not worked as intended, and has indeed produced levels of controversy and confusion," said Baker, who served under President George H.W. Bush. "Every president since its enactment has considered it unconstitutional, and it has been regularly ignored or circumvented."

## A New Consultative Framework

The centerpiece of the commission's recommendation is a proposed "War Powers Consultation Act" that would establish clearer procedures for communication between the branches of government before significant military engagements.

Under the proposal, the president would be required to consult with a newly created joint congressional committee before ordering significant armed conflict—defined as combat operations expected to last more than a week. The bill would also establish a permanent bipartisan congressional body specifically tasked with reviewing and responding to such decisions.

Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that the recommendation seeks a middle path.

"We are not trying to resolve the underlying constitutional questions that have divided presidents and Congress for generations," Christopher said. "Instead, we are proposing a practical mechanism that encourages genuine consultation while respecting the legitimate authorities of both branches."

## Addressing Decades of Dispute

The 1973 resolution was passed over President Richard Nixon's veto in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, as lawmakers sought to reassert congressional authority over military commitments. It requires presidents to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying forces and limits deployments to 60 days without congressional authorization.

However, critics across the political spectrum have long argued the law is fundamentally flawed. Presidents of both parties have questioned its constitutionality, while some lawmakers say it has actually ceded too much authority to the executive branch.

The commission's report notes that the resolution's requirements have been inconsistently observed through numerous military actions spanning multiple administrations.

## Reaction on Capitol Hill

The recommendations drew measured interest from lawmakers, though passage of any replacement legislation remains uncertain given the deeply rooted institutional and partisan tensions surrounding war powers.

Supporters of reform praised the commission's effort to break a long-standing impasse, while some legal scholars cautioned that no statute can fully resolve constitutional ambiguities that ultimately may require judicial or political resolution.

The commission included former legislators, government officials, and legal experts from both parties, lending its findings a degree of bipartisan credibility that its authors hope will encourage congressional action.

Whether Congress will take up the proposal remains to be seen, but the involvement of two respected former secretaries of state has ensured the recommendations will receive serious attention in Washington's ongoing debate over who holds the power to take the nation to war.

# National War Powers Commission Proposes Mandatory Congressional Consultation Before Military Action

## Bipartisan Panel Seeks to Resolve Decades-Long Constitutional Dispute Over War-Making Authority

**WASHINGTON** — A bipartisan commission of prominent former government officials and legal scholars has recommended sweeping changes to the way the United States decides to go to war, proposing legislation that would require the president to consult with Congress before committing American troops to significant armed conflict.

The National War Powers Commission, co-chaired by two former secretaries of state from opposing political parties, released its findings after more than a year of study, concluding that the existing War Powers Resolution of 1973 has proven ineffective and is widely regarded as unconstitutional by presidents of both parties.

## The Core Proposal

At the heart of the commission's recommendation is a proposed statute that would establish clear procedures for consultation between the executive and legislative branches before the nation enters major military engagements.

Under the proposed framework, the president would be required to consult with a newly created congressional body before ordering deployments expected to last longer than a week. The plan calls for the establishment of a Joint Congressional Consultation Committee, comprising leaders from both chambers and the ranking members of key committees, to serve as a permanent point of contact between the branches.

"The current law has not worked as intended," the commission stated in its report. "It has been regularly ignored, circumvented, or challenged since its passage over the veto of President Nixon."

## Voices from the Panel

The commission's co-chairs emphasized that the proposal was designed not to favor either branch of government, but to encourage genuine dialogue on matters of war and peace.

"After the tragedy of 9/11 and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, we thought it was important to have some clarity about how these decisions should be made," said one co-chair, a former secretary of state. "The Constitution's provisions on war powers have been debated for more than 200 years. We are not trying to resolve every constitutional question, but to create a practical mechanism that ensures both branches are engaged."

The other co-chair stressed the bipartisan nature of the effort. "This is not a Democratic proposal or a Republican proposal," he said. "It is an American proposal. Presidents of both parties have found the 1973 resolution unworkable, and members of Congress across the spectrum have felt sidelined in decisions that send our sons and daughters into harm's way."

A former attorney general who served on the panel addressed the legal reasoning behind the recommendation. "We deliberately avoided trying to define the precise boundaries of the president's constitutional authority as commander in chief, or of Congress's power to declare war," he explained. "Instead, we focused on process. If we can guarantee meaningful consultation, we believe better decisions will follow."

## Addressing the Shortcomings of Current Law

Panel members were pointed in their criticism of the existing statute, which requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing armed forces into hostilities and generally bars deployments lasting more than 60 days without congressional authorization.

"Every president since Nixon has taken the position that the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional, at least in part," noted one legal scholar on the commission. "When a law is routinely disregarded by the very officials it is meant to govern, that law has failed in its essential purpose."

Another commissioner, a veteran of congressional service, said the reform aimed to restore Congress's rightful role. "The framers gave the power to declare war to the legislative branch for a reason," she said. "They understood that such momentous decisions should not rest with a single individual. Our proposal seeks to honor that vision while acknowledging the realities of modern warfare, where rapid response is sometimes essential."

## Key Provisions

According to the report, the proposed legislation would:

- **Require consultation** with the Joint Congressional Consultation Committee before any "significant armed conflict," defined as combat operations lasting or expected to last more than one week.

- **Establish a permanent committee** to facilitate ongoing communication and provide Congress with timely access to information.

- **Mandate a congressional vote** within 30 days on a resolution of approval, ensuring that lawmakers go on record supporting or opposing military action.

- **Provide exceptions** for emergencies, allowing the president to act first and consult within three days when circumstances demand immediate action.

## Reaction and the Road Ahead

The commission acknowledged that turning its recommendations into law would require significant political will. Some constitutional experts not involved with the panel have already questioned whether any statute can truly bind a president's exercise of commander-in-chief powers.

"No law can force a president to genuinely listen," one commissioner conceded. "But by creating a structured, transparent process, we increase the likelihood that consultation will be substantive rather than perfunctory. That is a meaningful improvement over the status quo."

The co-chairs indicated they would present their proposal to congressional leaders and the White House in the coming weeks, expressing hope that the measure could attract support across party lines.

"We offer this not as the final word, but as a starting point for a serious national conversation," the first co-chair said. "The question of how a democracy decides to go to war is among the most important any nation can face. It deserves our most careful attention."

*The commission's full report, along with the text of its proposed statute, has been made available for public review.*

---

*Note: This article is written as a general template based on the structure of the real National War Powers Commission, which was convened by the Miller Center at the University of Virginia and released its report in 2008. Specific quotes have been composed for illustrative purposes and should be verified against the actual report before publication.*

# Bipartisan Panel Urges Congress to Reclaim War Powers, Overhaul Decades-Old Framework

*Commission recommends replacing the 1973 War Powers Resolution with stricter mechanisms to check executive military authority*

WASHINGTON — A bipartisan commission of former lawmakers, legal scholars, and national security officials released a comprehensive report this week calling for a fundamental overhaul of the laws governing how the United States goes to war, arguing that Congress has ceded too much authority to the executive branch over half a century of expanding presidential military action.

The panel's recommendations, the product of an eighteen-month review, aim to address what its members describe as a persistent imbalance between the legislative and executive branches—one that has allowed presidents of both parties to commit American forces to hostilities abroad with minimal congressional input.

## A Framework Under Strain

At the center of the debate is the War Powers Resolution of 1973, a law born from the political turmoil of the Vietnam War era. Passed over President Richard Nixon's veto, the resolution was Congress's attempt to reassert its constitutional authority to declare war after successive presidents had escalated the conflict in Southeast Asia without formal legislative approval.

The Constitution divides war powers between the branches. Article I grants Congress the power to "declare War" and to raise and fund armies, while Article II designates the president as "Commander in Chief" of the armed forces. For much of American history, this division created tension that was managed through political practice rather than firm legal rules.

The 1973 resolution sought to codify limits. Its key provision requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing armed forces into hostilities and prohibits military engagement from extending beyond 60 days—with a 30-day withdrawal period—unless Congress authorizes the action or declares war.

But critics across the political spectrum have long argued that the law has failed in practice. Presidents have generally treated the notification requirement as a procedural formality while disputing the constitutionality of the 60-day clock. Congress, for its part, has rarely mustered the political will to enforce the resolution's limits or to formally authorize—or halt—military operations.

"The War Powers Resolution has become a statute honored more in the breach than in the observance," said one commission member, a former legal adviser who served in Republican and Democratic administrations. "Both branches have found it convenient to leave the hard questions unanswered."

## Decades of Expanding Executive Action

The panel's report traces how military engagements over the past several decades have stretched the boundaries of executive authority. It points to operations conducted without explicit congressional approval and to the expansive use of two authorizations for the use of military force, or AUMFs, passed in 2001 and 2002.

The 2001 authorization, enacted days after the September 11 attacks, empowered the president to pursue those responsible for the attacks and those who harbored them. In the years since, it has been cited as legal justification for military operations against numerous groups in multiple countries—many with only tenuous connections to the original perpetrators. The 2002 authorization, which cleared the way for the invasion of Iraq, has remained on the books long after the conflict it addressed concluded.

"These authorizations have taken on lives their authors never envisioned," the report states. "A statute passed to address a specific threat has been transformed into a standing grant of authority spanning administrations and continents."

## The Panel's Recommendations

The commission's proposals seek to replace the existing framework with mechanisms designed to be more enforceable and harder for either branch to ignore.

**Repealing outdated authorizations.** The panel calls for the immediate repeal of the 2002 Iraq authorization, which it describes as obsolete. It further recommends that the 2001 authorization be subjected to a "sunset" provision, requiring Congress to affirmatively reauthorize it at regular intervals or allow it to expire.

**Automatic funding cutoffs.** In perhaps its most consequential recommendation, the commission proposes that unauthorized military engagements automatically lose funding after a set period unless Congress votes affirmatively to continue them. By tying the enforcement mechanism to the appropriations power—an authority the executive cannot circumvent—the panel hopes to give the time limits genuine force. Under the current law, inaction by Congress effectively allows operations to continue; the proposed reform would reverse that default.

**A clearer definition of "hostilities."** The report addresses a recurring source of dispute: what actually triggers the law's requirements. Administrations have argued that certain operations—including airstrikes, drone campaigns, and support for allied forces—do not constitute "hostilities" within the meaning of the resolution. The panel recommends a broadened and more precise definition to close what it calls "interpretive loopholes."

**Expedited judicial review.** To overcome courts' historical reluctance to intervene in war powers disputes, which judges have often dismissed as "political questions," the commission proposes granting a defined group of legislators standing to bring challenges and establishing an expedited process for judicial resolution.

**Consultation requirements.** Beyond notification, the panel recommends meaningful advance consultation with a designated congressional leadership group before the commitment of forces, except in cases of genuine emergency requiring immediate action to repel an attack.

## Prospects and Skepticism

Whether the recommendations will gain traction on Capitol Hill remains uncertain. Efforts to reform war powers have surfaced repeatedly over the years, occasionally advancing through committee or securing floor votes, but comprehensive reform has consistently stalled.

The obstacles are both institutional and political. Presidents of both parties have resisted measures they view as encroaching on their constitutional prerogatives as commander in chief. And lawmakers, while often eager to criticize executive overreach, have sometimes proven reluctant to accept the accountability that comes with formally authorizing—or refusing to authorize—the use of force.

"There's a certain comfort in ambiguity," a former member of Congress who served on the panel observed. "It allows legislators to claim credit when operations succeed and to disclaim responsibility when they don't. Real reform requires giving that up."

Constitutional scholars are divided on some of the panel's proposals. Some question whether provisions granting legislators standing to sue would survive judicial scrutiny, given courts' longstanding hesitancy in this area. Others argue that the fundamental problem is not the adequacy of the law but the absence of political will to use the tools Congress already possesses, including its power over the purse.

Supporters counter that the current arrangement is untenable. "The framers deliberately made the decision to go to war difficult, requiring the assent of the people's representatives," the report concludes. "A system in which that decision rests effectively with a single individual is not the one they designed."

## An Enduring Constitutional Question

The commission's work enters a long-running debate that predates the 1973 resolution and is likely to outlast any single reform effort. At its core lie questions the Constitution left in productive tension: how a democracy balances the need for decisive action against threats with the requirement that decisions of war and peace reflect broad democratic consent.

For now, the panel's report adds a detailed and bipartisan voice to the argument that the balance has drifted too far toward the executive—and offers a concrete roadmap for those in Congress willing to take up the challenge of reclaiming a power the legislative branch has, over decades, largely allowed to slip away.

Whether lawmakers will act on that roadmap, the panel's members acknowledge, is a question that only Congress itself can answer.

---

*Note: This article is a general journalistic treatment of presidential war powers reform. It describes the historical framework accurately but presents a composite "panel" and its recommendations as an illustrative example rather than a report on a specific, named commission.*

# Blue-Ribbon Panel Urges Overhaul of War Powers Framework, Citing Decades of Presidential Overreach

**WASHINGTON** — A bipartisan commission of former officials, legal scholars, and military experts released findings this week calling for a fundamental reform of the legal framework governing how the United States goes to war, concluding that the current system has failed to preserve Congress's constitutional role in decisions to commit American forces to combat.

The panel's report examined the persistent tension between the executive and legislative branches over war-making authority, focusing particular attention on the 1973 War Powers Resolution and the authorizations for military force that have shaped U.S. conflicts over the past two decades.

## Background on the 1973 Law

The War Powers Resolution was enacted in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, passed by Congress over President Richard Nixon's veto. The law was designed to check the president's ability to commit U.S. forces to hostilities without congressional approval.

Under its provisions, a president must notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing armed forces into hostilities and must terminate military action within 60 to 90 days absent congressional authorization.

Yet, as the panel noted, virtually every president since its passage—regardless of party—has regarded the resolution as an unconstitutional infringement on the commander-in-chief powers granted by Article II. Presidents have frequently complied with the law's reporting requirements while simultaneously asserting they were not legally bound to do so, creating what the report described as a "constitutional gray zone" that has persisted for half a century.

## The 2002 Iraq Resolution

The commission devoted significant attention to the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, which Congress passed to authorize the invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.

That authorization, the panel observed, remained on the books long after its original purpose had been fulfilled, illustrating a broader problem with open-ended war authorizations. Along with the 2001 authorization passed after the September 11 attacks, these measures have been cited by multiple administrations to justify military operations far beyond their initial scope and against adversaries that did not exist when the resolutions were written.

The report noted that efforts to repeal the 2002 authorization have gained bipartisan momentum in recent years, with lawmakers arguing that leaving obsolete war authorizations in place invites their misuse by the executive branch.

## The Panel's Recommendations

Among its central recommendations, the commission called on Congress to:

- **Repeal outdated authorizations**, including the 2002 Iraq measure, and establish sunset provisions requiring future authorizations to expire unless renewed.
- **Clarify the War Powers Resolution's triggers** to reduce ambiguity over what constitutes "hostilities," a term successive administrations have interpreted narrowly to avoid the law's constraints.
- **Strengthen reporting and consultation requirements** to ensure meaningful legislative input before, not merely after, forces are committed.

The panel warned that congressional reluctance to assert its authority—as much as executive ambition—has contributed to the erosion of the constitutional balance. "The accumulation of war powers in the presidency has been enabled by legislative acquiescence," the report stated.

Whether Congress will act on the recommendations remains uncertain. Similar reform efforts have repeatedly stalled, and lawmakers have often proven reluctant to take politically difficult votes on the use of military force.

*This is a general summary of the type of findings such panels typically produce. For coverage of a specific commission or report, additional details would be needed.*
